Option C adds API Gateway between every service pair which is architecturally impractical for microservices. Option D uses Istio which is designed for Kubernetes, not native ECS Fargate integration.

stem: A company wants to implement trunk-based development where all developers commit to the main branch. Feature flags control the visibility of incomplete features. The team needs a managed service to control feature flags with gradual rollout percentages and instant kill-switch capability. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this use case?

options.text: Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to store feature flag values as JSON StringList parameters. Configure each application to poll Parameter Store every 30 seconds and parse the JSON to determine feature visibility based on user ID hashing.

Use AWS Lambda@Edge functions integrated with CloudFront to evaluate feature flags at the edge. Store flag configurations in an S3 bucket as JSON files and have Lambda@Edge read the flags to modify response headers that control feature visibility in the client application.

Use Amazon DynamoDB with a feature flags table containing flag name, enabled status, and rollout percentage attributes. Implement a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster for low-latency reads and use DynamoDB Streams to propagate flag changes to application instances.

Use AWS AppConfig with feature flag configuration profiles. Define each feature as a flag with a percentage-based deployment strategy, and configure the AppConfig Lambda extension in each service to retrieve flag values with local caching and instant flag updates.

explanation: AWS AppConfig natively supports feature flags with percentage-based rollouts, validation, and deployment strategies. The Lambda extension provides local caching with near-instant flag updates when changed. Option B requires custom implementation for percentage rollout and doesn't have native feature flag support. Option C builds a custom feature flag system on DynamoDB, adding unnecessary infrastructure management. Option D processes flags at the CDN edge which doesn't support server-side feature toggling for backend services.

stem: A company needs to create a self-service provisioning system where development teams can request pre-approved infrastructure templates through a service catalog. The system must enforce tagging standards, limit instance types, and track costs per team. Which AWS service combination provides this governed self-service capability?

options.text: Deploy AWS Control Tower with Account Factory to provision development team accounts. Use Control Tower guardrails to enforce instance type restrictions and tagging standards, and provide teams with pre-configured account vending machine templates for infrastructure.

Create a custom web portal using API Gateway and Lambda that presents a list of approved CloudFormation templates stored in S3. Implement Lambda functions that deploy stacks with mandatory tags and validate instance types against an approved list before provisioning.

Configure AWS Organizations with SCPs that restrict resource creation to approved instance types only. Create shared CloudFormation templates in a central S3 bucket accessible to all accounts and rely on SCPs to enforce tagging through condition keys in the policies.

Deploy AWS Service Catalog with portfolios containing approved CloudFormation products. Apply launch constraints with IAM roles that enforce tagging through CloudFormation stack policies, and configure TagOptions to require team and cost-center tags on all provisioned resources.

explanation: AWS Service Catalog provides governed self-service provisioning with portfolios, launch constraints, and TagOptions for mandatory tagging. Teams can only launch pre-approved products with enforced guardrails. Option B builds a custom portal that duplicates Service Catalog functionality without its governance features. Option C uses SCPs for enforcement but doesn't provide a self-service catalog interface for teams. Option D provides account-level governance but doesn't offer per-resource self-service provisioning with product catalogs.

stem: A company runs a containerized application on Amazon EKS that must maintain 99.99% availability. The application uses persistent volumes backed by Amazon EBS. During an AZ outage, pods with EBS volumes could not be rescheduled to another AZ because EBS volumes are AZ-specific. Which solution ensures pod reschedulability across AZs?

options.text: Enable EBS Multi-Attach on io2 volumes to allow the same volume to be attached to instances in multiple AZs simultaneously. Update the PersistentVolume accessMode to ReadWriteMany and configure the StatefulSet to use a podAntiAffinity rule spreading replicas across AZs.

Configure EBS volume snapshots on a 5-minute schedule using AWS Backup. Deploy a custom Kubernetes operator that detects AZ failures, creates new EBS volumes from the latest snapshot in the healthy AZ, and patches PersistentVolume definitions to reference the new volumes.

Replace EBS-backed PersistentVolumes with Amazon EFS-backed PersistentVolumes using the EFS CSI driver. Configure the EFS file system with mount targets in all cluster AZs and set the StorageClass reclaim policy to Retain for data persistence across pod rescheduling.

Deploy the application using a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates and configure topology-aware volume provisioning. Set the StatefulSet's podManagementPolicy to Parallel and use the EBS CSI driver's topology constraints to create volumes in the same AZ as scheduled pods.

explanation: Amazon EFS provides multi-AZ storage accessible from any AZ, allowing pods to be rescheduled to any AZ without volume constraints. The EFS CSI driver integrates natively with Kubernetes PersistentVolumes. Option B uses snapshots which introduces data loss (up to 5 minutes) and requires custom operator complexity. Option C is incorrect because EBS Multi-Attach only works within the same AZ, not across AZs. Option D keeps EBS which remains AZ-bound and doesn't solve the cross-AZ rescheduling problem.

stem: A company's Lambda functions write structured JSON logs to CloudWatch Logs. The operations team wants to create metric filters that extract business metrics like order amounts and processing times from the log entries, and alarm when the average order processing time exceeds 3 seconds over a 5-minute period. Which approach is MOST efficient?

options.text: Create a Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream subscribed to the CloudWatch log groups. Configure a Lambda transformation function to parse JSON logs, extract metrics, and call the CloudWatch PutMetricData API to publish custom metrics before forwarding logs to S3.

Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to run scheduled queries every 5 minutes that parse the JSON logs and compute average processing times. Configure the scheduled query to publish results as custom metrics and create alarms on the query result metrics.

Modify the Lambda functions to use the CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF) to publish processingTime and orderAmount as custom metrics directly within log entries. Create CloudWatch alarms on the automatically generated metrics without needing separate metric filters.

Use CloudWatch Logs metric filters with JSON filter pattern syntax to extract the processingTime field from structured log entries. Create a custom CloudWatch metric from the extracted values and configure a CloudWatch alarm on the Average statistic with a 5-minute period.

explanation: CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF) generates custom metrics directly from structured log output without separate metric filters. Metrics are automatically created with dimensions and appear in CloudWatch Metrics for alarming. Option A works but requires creating and maintaining separate metric filters outside the application code. Option C introduces unnecessary Kinesis infrastructure for metric extraction. Option D uses scheduled queries which have minimum 1-hour evaluation intervals and are not designed for real-time alarming.

stem: A company uses Amazon Route 53 with health checks to route traffic between two Regions. The health check monitors an HTTP endpoint on port 443. During a recent certificate renewal, the health check temporarily failed because the new certificate's Subject Alternative Name didn't match the health check's configured FQDN. How should the team prevent this from recurring?

options.text: Configure the Route 53 health check to use the EnableSNI setting with the FullyQualifiedDomainName matching the certificate's SAN. Use AWS Certificate Manager to manage certificate renewals with automatic renewal enabled, ensuring SANs are preserved during renewal.

Configure the Route 53 health check to use a calculated health check that combines an HTTPS check with a TCP port 443 check. Set the health check routing to failover only when both child checks report unhealthy, preventing certificate-only failures from triggering failover.

Change the Route 53 health check from HTTPS to TCP on port 443 to bypass SSL certificate validation entirely. Configure the health check with a request interval of 10 seconds and a failure threshold of 3 to quickly detect genuine endpoint failures without certificate issues.

Create a CloudWatch alarm that monitors the ACM certificate expiration DaysToExpiry metric. Configure an EventBridge rule to trigger a Lambda function that updates the Route 53 health check FQDN to match the new certificate's SAN before certificate renewal completes.

explanation: Route 53 health checks support SNI and FQDN configuration for proper SSL validation. Using ACM with automatic renewal preserves SANs, preventing mismatches. Option B bypasses SSL validation which removes a security layer and doesn't verify the endpoint is fully functional. Option C creates a workaround that masks genuine certificate issues. Option D adds complexity and race conditions between certificate renewal and health check updates.

stem: A financial services company needs to implement network segmentation for its VPC to isolate the web tier, application tier, and database tier. Each tier must only be able to communicate with its adjacent tier, and all inter-tier traffic must be logged. Which architecture implements this network segmentation?

options.text: Place each tier in separate subnets with Network ACLs configured to allow traffic only between adjacent tier subnets. Enable VPC Flow Logs on all subnet ENIs and configure the flow logs to publish to a CloudWatch log group with a 1-minute aggregation interval.

Place each tier in separate subnets with security groups that reference adjacent tier security group IDs as allowed sources. Deploy AWS Network Firewall between tiers with stateful rules logging allowed and denied traffic to a centralized S3 bucket via Firehose.

Deploy each tier in a separate subnet and use AWS PrivateLink to create VPC endpoints between adjacent tiers. Configure endpoint policies to restrict access to specific service actions and enable CloudTrail logging for all VPC endpoint API calls.

Deploy each tier in a separate VPC connected via VPC peering with non-overlapping CIDR blocks. Configure security groups to allow traffic only from the peered VPC's CIDR range and enable VPC Flow Logs on the peering connection ENIs for traffic logging.

explanation: Security groups referencing adjacent tier SG IDs enforce communication only between adjacent tiers. AWS Network Firewall provides stateful inspection and centralized logging of all inter-tier traffic. Option A uses NACLs which are stateless and harder to manage, and don't provide deep packet inspection logging. Option B over-engineers with separate VPCs for tiers within the same application. Option D uses PrivateLink which is designed for service-to-service private connectivity, not general inter-tier communication.

stem: A company needs to implement automated testing in their CI/CD pipeline that validates infrastructure changes before deployment. The tests must verify that a CloudFormation template creates the expected resources with correct configurations, without actually deploying resources to AWS. Which testing approach satisfies this requirement?

options.text: Use TaskCat in a CodeBuild stage to test CloudFormation templates across multiple Regions simultaneously. Configure TaskCat with test parameters for each Region and validate that stacks create successfully and output values match expected results before deletion.

Deploy the CloudFormation template to a dedicated testing account using a CodePipeline stage. Run integration tests against the deployed resources using a CodeBuild project, then delete the test stack and promote the template to production if tests pass.

Use the CloudFormation Linter (cfn-lint) in a CodeBuild stage to validate template syntax and check against the CloudFormation resource specification. Add cfn-nag for security scanning and integrate both tools as build steps that fail the pipeline on errors or warnings.

Write unit tests using the CDK assertions library or cfn-guard policy-as-code rules to validate the synthesized CloudFormation template. Run the tests in a CodeBuild stage to verify resource counts, property values, and security configurations without deploying to AWS.

explanation: CDK assertions library and cfn-guard validate template structure and configurations without deploying resources, providing true unit testing of infrastructure code. Option A validates syntax and security patterns but doesn't verify resource configurations against expected values. Option B deploys actual resources which violates the 'without actually deploying' requirement. Option C also deploys real stacks in test Regions, which provisions actual resources.

stem: A company uses AWS CloudFormation custom resources backed by Lambda functions to configure third-party SaaS integrations during stack creation. The custom resource Lambda function occasionally times out after 15 minutes, causing stack creation to hang for hours until the custom resource times out. Which approach resolves the timeout issue?

options.text: Increase the Lambda function timeout to the maximum of 15 minutes and add retry logic with exponential backoff within the handler. Configure the Lambda to send a FAILED response to CloudFormation's pre-signed S3 URL if the operation exceeds a configured time limit.

Implement the custom resource as an asynchronous workflow using Step Functions. Have the Lambda function start the Step Functions execution and immediately return SUCCESS to CloudFormation, while the state machine handles the SaaS integration with built-in retry logic.

Configure the custom resource with a ServiceTimeout property set to 20 minutes to extend the wait period. Add a CloudWatch alarm on the Lambda function Duration metric that triggers an SNS notification if execution time approaches the Lambda 15-minute timeout limit.

Replace the Lambda-backed custom resource with an AWS CloudFormation macro that transforms the template to include the SaaS integration configuration. Run the macro during template processing to avoid runtime timeouts during stack creation operations.

explanation: Lambda must always send a response (SUCCESS or FAILED) to CloudFormation's pre-signed URL before timing out. Adding a time limit check within the handler that sends FAILED before Lambda timeout prevents CloudFormation from hanging. Option B uses macros which run during template processing and can't perform runtime API calls to SaaS services. Option C returns SUCCESS immediately which means CloudFormation proceeds without knowing if the SaaS integration actually succeeded. Option D's ServiceTimeout doesn't exist as a custom resource property.

stem: A company runs a message processing application that reads from an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream with 10 shards. During peak hours, the consumer Lambda function falls behind, causing the iterator age to exceed 1 hour. The team needs to increase throughput without modifying the producer application. Which solution addresses the consumer lag?

options.text: Enable enhanced fan-out on the Kinesis stream for the consumer Lambda function. This provides a dedicated 2 MB/s read throughput per shard, eliminating contention with other consumers and significantly improving the read rate for the lagging consumer application.

Replace the Lambda consumer with an ECS Fargate service using the Kinesis Client Library (KCL). Configure the KCL application with a DynamoDB lease table and set the maxRecords per GetRecords call to 10000 for higher per-shard throughput.

Configure the Lambda event source mapping with a batch size of 10000 records and a maximum batching window of 5 seconds. Increase the Lambda function memory to 10240 MB to improve CPU allocation and enable provisioned concurrency matching the shard count.

Increase the number of shards in the Kinesis stream from 10 to 20 using the UpdateShardCount API. Update the Lambda event source mapping to increase the parallelization factor, allowing multiple Lambda invocations to process each shard simultaneously.

explanation: Increasing shards doubles the stream's read/write capacity, and the parallelization factor allows multiple Lambda invocations per shard, addressing both throughput and processing capacity. Option A provides dedicated throughput but doesn't increase the processing parallelism of the Lambda consumer. Option C adjusts batch parameters but doesn't address the fundamental throughput limitation of 10 shards. Option D migrates to ECS/KCL which doesn't inherently provide more throughput than Lambda with proper configuration.

stem: A company needs to monitor the health of 300 API endpoints across multiple AWS accounts and Regions. Each endpoint must be checked every 30 seconds, and the team needs a single dashboard showing endpoint availability, latency, and SSL certificate expiration. Which solution provides this consolidated monitoring?

options.text: Use AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) collectors deployed as ECS Fargate tasks in each Region. Configure HTTP check receivers to probe endpoints every 30 seconds and export metrics to Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus with a centralized Grafana dashboard.

Create Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries for each endpoint using the heartbeat monitoring blueprint. Configure canary schedules to run every 1 minute and publish metrics to CloudWatch. Use CloudWatch cross-account observability to aggregate metrics in a central monitoring account.

Deploy a fleet of EC2 instances in each Region running a custom health check script that tests each endpoint every 30 seconds. Publish results as CloudWatch custom metrics using the PutMetricData API with dimensions for account, Region, and endpoint name.

Configure Route 53 health checks for each endpoint with a 30-second request interval. Enable health check CloudWatch metrics and create a CloudWatch dashboard in the us-east-1 Region displaying all health check metrics including latency and SSL certificate DaysToExpiry.

explanation: Route 53 health checks natively support 30-second intervals, measure latency, report SSL expiry days, and publish metrics to CloudWatch in us-east-1. This provides a managed solution with minimal operational overhead. Option A uses Synthetics canaries which have a minimum interval of 1 minute, not 30 seconds. Option B requires managing custom EC2 infrastructure across Regions. Option D adds complexity with OpenTelemetry and Prometheus when Route 53 provides the exact required functionality natively.

stem: A company's EC2-based application suddenly started returning HTTP 500 errors after a configuration change pushed via AWS Systems Manager State Manager. The team needs to quickly revert to the previous configuration. The State Manager association applied an SSM document that modified application configuration files on 200 instances. Which approach provides the fastest rollback?

options.text: Use SSM Run Command to execute a command document that restores the configuration files from a backup stored in S3. Set MaxConcurrency to 100% and MaxErrors to 0 to apply the rollback to all 200 instances simultaneously with immediate failure detection.

Create an SSM Automation document that connects to each instance via Session Manager and reverts the configuration file changes. Execute the Automation document with a rate control of 50 instances at a time and a failure threshold of 5% across the fleet.

Terminate all 200 instances and allow the Auto Scaling group to launch replacements with the original launch template UserData. Configure the Auto Scaling group's instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of 90% to maintain availability during replacement.

Create a new version of the SSM document containing the previous configuration values. Update the State Manager association to use the new document version and wait for the association to automatically re-apply across all 200 instances at the next scheduled interval.

explanation: SSM Run Command with 100% MaxConcurrency executes the rollback on all instances immediately, providing the fastest restoration. Backup files in S3 provide the known-good configuration. Option A waits for the next scheduled association interval which delays rollback. Option C terminates instances causing downtime during replacement even with 90% minimum healthy percentage. Option D uses Automation which adds orchestration overhead and rate-limited execution when speed is critical.

stem: A company needs to implement a centralized secrets management solution for applications running across 20 AWS accounts. Secrets must be encrypted with account-specific KMS keys, rotated automatically, and access must be auditable. Which TWO configurations are required?

options.text: Deploy AWS Secrets Manager in each account with account-specific KMS CMKs for encryption. Enable automatic rotation using Lambda functions deployed in each account's VPC and configure rotation schedules based on the sensitivity classification of each secret.

Enable AWS CloudTrail in all accounts with data events for Secrets Manager API calls. Create a centralized CloudTrail trail that aggregates logs to a security account's S3 bucket, and configure CloudWatch Logs metric filters to alert on unauthorized GetSecretValue calls.

Create a centralized Secrets Manager instance in a shared services account with a single KMS CMK. Configure resource-based policies on each secret to grant cross-account access and share secrets using AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) for simplified management.

Deploy HashiCorp Vault on ECS Fargate in the shared services account with transit encryption enabled. Configure Vault's AWS auth backend to authenticate applications from each account and use Vault's built-in audit logging to record all secret access events.

explanation: Secrets Manager in each account with account-specific KMS keys provides isolation and automatic rotation (A). CloudTrail with data events for Secrets Manager provides the audit trail for all secret access across accounts (C). Option B uses a centralized approach but RAM doesn't support Secrets Manager sharing, and a single KMS key violates the account-specific encryption requirement. Option D introduces third-party infrastructure when native AWS services meet all requirements.

stem: A development team wants to implement canary deployments for their Lambda functions using AWS SAM. The deployment should shift 10% of traffic to the new version, monitor for errors for 5 minutes, then shift the remaining 90% if no errors occur. Which SAM configuration implements this?

options.text: Configure the Lambda function with two versions behind an Application Load Balancer target group using weighted target groups. Set the primary target group weight to 90% and the canary target group to 10%, with ALB health checks triggering automatic deregistration.

Configure the Lambda function's DeploymentPreference property with Type set to Canary10Percent5Minutes. Define pre-traffic and post-traffic hooks as Lambda functions and add CloudWatch alarms monitoring the Lambda Errors metric for automatic rollback on failures.

Configure the Lambda function with a provisioned concurrency setting of 10% on the new version. Create an API Gateway canary deployment stage that routes 10% of traffic and use a Step Functions workflow to promote or rollback after a 5-minute evaluation.

Create a Lambda alias with a routing configuration that sends 10% of invocations to the new version. Configure a CloudWatch Events rule to trigger a Lambda function after 5 minutes that updates the alias routing to 100% or rolls back based on error metric evaluation.

explanation: SAM's DeploymentPreference with Canary10Percent5Minutes natively implements the canary pattern using CodeDeploy, including traffic shifting, monitoring, and automatic rollback via CloudWatch alarms. Option B uses provisioned concurrency which controls cold starts, not traffic routing, and requires custom orchestration. Option C manually implements canary logic that SAM handles natively. Option D uses ALB routing which is for HTTP workloads and doesn't apply to general Lambda function invocations.

stem: A company manages 100 CloudFormation stacks across multiple accounts. They frequently need to update a common parameter (like AMI ID) across all stacks when a new golden AMI is released. Manual updates are error-prone and time-consuming. Which approach automates this cross-stack parameter update?

options.text: Store the AMI ID in a DynamoDB global table replicated across all accounts' Regions. Use CloudFormation custom resources backed by Lambda functions that query DynamoDB for the current AMI ID during stack creation and update operations.

Store the AMI ID in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as a public parameter. Reference the parameter in all CloudFormation templates using the AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value dynamic reference. When the parameter is updated, trigger stack updates across all accounts via CodePipeline.

Create a CloudFormation StackSet that deploys a common parameter stack to all accounts. Use cross-stack references with Fn::ImportValue in each application stack to reference the AMI ID. Update the StackSet to propagate the new AMI ID to all accounts automatically.

Use AWS Service Catalog with a central AMI portfolio that publishes the latest AMI ID as a product output. Configure dependent stacks to reference the Service Catalog product output and trigger product updates to propagate the new AMI ID to all provisioned products.

explanation: SSM Parameter Store with dynamic references in CloudFormation allows centralized parameter management. Updating the parameter and triggering stack updates via CodePipeline automates the process. Option B uses cross-stack references which create hard dependencies and can't easily propagate updates to existing stacks. Option C adds Service Catalog complexity for a simple parameter update use case. Option D requires custom resources and DynamoDB global tables which adds significant infrastructure overhead.

stem: A company's microservices architecture uses Amazon API Gateway as the front door. During a downstream service outage, API Gateway continued forwarding requests, causing cascading failures across multiple services. Which pattern prevents cascading failures in this architecture?

options.text: Configure API Gateway with Lambda authorizers that check downstream service health before routing requests. Cache health check results for 30 seconds and return HTTP 503 with a Retry-After header when the downstream service is detected as unhealthy.

Deploy AWS App Mesh with circuit breaker configuration on each virtual node's outlier detection settings. Configure connection pool limits, pending request thresholds, and consecutive error counts that trigger the circuit breaker to stop sending traffic to failing services.

Implement bulkhead isolation by deploying each downstream service behind a separate Network Load Balancer. Configure NLB cross-zone load balancing and target group health checks with a 5-second interval to quickly detect and isolate failing service instances.

Implement circuit breaker pattern using API Gateway usage plans with throttling limits per downstream service. Configure burst and rate limits based on each service's capacity and return HTTP 429 responses when limits are exceeded to protect downstream services.

explanation: AWS App Mesh provides native circuit breaker functionality through outlier detection, which stops routing traffic to failing services based on consecutive errors and connection thresholds. Option A uses throttling/rate limiting which controls request volume but doesn't implement circuit breaking based on error rates. Option C adds custom health check logic in authorizers which is not their intended purpose. Option D uses separate NLBs for isolation but doesn't implement the circuit breaker pattern that stops traffic to failing services.

stem: A company runs a data pipeline that processes files uploaded to S3, transforms them using Lambda, and stores results in DynamoDB. The operations team needs to track the end-to-end processing time for each file and identify bottlenecks. Some files take 10x longer than average. Which observability approach best identifies the processing bottlenecks?

options.text: Configure CloudWatch Container Insights for the Lambda function to collect per-invocation metrics including duration, memory usage, and initialization time. Create a CloudWatch dashboard with percentile statistics showing p99 duration and correlate with file size dimensions.

Configure Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus to scrape custom metrics from the Lambda function using the Prometheus client library. Define recording rules to compute processing duration histograms by file type and size bucket, and visualize in Grafana dashboards.

Enable S3 event notifications to publish to CloudWatch Logs via an SNS topic. Create Lambda function CloudWatch Logs metric filters that extract processing duration and file metadata, then build CloudWatch Logs Insights queries to analyze slow file processing patterns.

Enable AWS X-Ray tracing on the Lambda function and instrument the code with custom subsegments for each processing stage. Annotate traces with the S3 object key and file size, then use X-Ray analytics to filter traces by duration and identify slow processing stages.

explanation: X-Ray tracing with custom subsegments provides granular visibility into each processing stage within a Lambda invocation. Annotations enable filtering by file attributes to identify patterns in slow processing. Option B provides aggregate Lambda metrics but doesn't show internal processing stage breakdowns. Option C uses log-based metrics which lack the trace-level granularity needed to identify specific bottleneck stages. Option D adds external monitoring infrastructure when X-Ray provides native serverless tracing.

stem: A company's production environment experienced a memory leak in an EC2 application that gradually consumed all available memory over 4 hours before the instance became unresponsive. CloudWatch basic monitoring with 5-minute metrics didn't detect the gradual increase early enough. Which monitoring improvement provides earlier detection?

options.text: Configure Amazon EventBridge with a scheduled rule that invokes a Lambda function every minute to query EC2 instance status checks. Publish custom metrics for StatusCheckFailed_Instance and create an alarm that triggers when status checks fail for 3 consecutive checks.

Enable AWS Systems Manager inventory collection on all EC2 instances with a custom inventory type for memory statistics. Configure SSM State Manager to collect memory data every 5 minutes and create an AWS Config rule that evaluates memory thresholds for compliance.

Install the CloudWatch agent on all EC2 instances configured to collect memory utilization at 1-minute intervals. Create a CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm on the mem_used_percent metric that triggers when memory usage deviates from the expected baseline pattern.

Enable EC2 detailed monitoring to collect CPU metrics at 1-minute intervals instead of the default 5-minute interval. Create a CloudWatch alarm on the CPUUtilization metric with anomaly detection bands and set the alarm to trigger when CPU exceeds normal patterns.

explanation: The CloudWatch agent provides memory metrics (not available via basic monitoring) and anomaly detection identifies gradual trends that static thresholds miss. Option B enables detailed CPU monitoring but memory metrics aren't included in EC2 basic or detailed monitoring. Option C checks instance status which only fails after the instance is completely unresponsive, too late for early detection. Option D uses inventory collection which doesn't support real-time metric alerting.

stem: A company needs to implement a policy that prevents any IAM user or role from creating resources outside of the approved AWS Regions (us-east-1 and eu-west-1), except for global services like IAM, CloudFront, and Route 53. Which mechanism enforces this restriction across all accounts?

options.text: Configure AWS Config rules that evaluate resource compliance by checking the Region attribute of every resource. Enable auto-remediation using SSM Automation to terminate or delete resources created in non-approved Regions and notify administrators via SNS.

Create an IAM permissions boundary policy that denies actions outside us-east-1 and eu-west-1 using the aws:RequestedRegion condition key. Attach the permissions boundary to all IAM users and roles in each account and exclude global service actions from the deny statement.

Create an SCP in AWS Organizations that denies all actions with a StringNotEquals condition on aws:RequestedRegion for us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Add a NotAction list for global services including iam:*, cloudfront:*, route53:*, and sts:* to exempt them from the Region restriction.

Deploy VPC configurations only in us-east-1 and eu-west-1, leaving other Regions without networking infrastructure. Create IAM policies that deny ec2:CreateVpc and ec2:CreateSubnet in all Regions to prevent teams from establishing networking in unapproved Regions.

explanation: SCPs enforce Region restrictions at the organization level across all accounts. Using NotAction for global services ensures IAM, CloudFront, Route 53, and STS continue to work regardless of Region. Option B uses permissions boundaries which must be attached individually and don't apply to root users. Option C detects after creation rather than preventing creation. Option D restricts only VPC creation and doesn't prevent other resource types from being created in non-approved Regions.

stem: A company uses AWS CodePipeline for continuous delivery. The production deployment stage requires approval from at least two different team leads within a 4-hour window. If only one approval is received, the deployment should be rejected. Which configuration implements this dual-approval requirement?

options.text: Add a single manual approval action in CodePipeline with an SNS topic that notifies both team leads. Configure a Lambda function as the approval reviewer that tracks approvals in a DynamoDB table and only approves the action when two distinct approvers have responded.

Replace the CodePipeline manual approval with an EventBridge rule that triggers a Step Functions workflow. The workflow sends approval requests via SNS, waits for two callback tokens from distinct approvers within 4 hours, and calls PutApprovalResult on success.

Add two sequential manual approval actions in the production stage of CodePipeline, each assigned to a different SNS topic subscribed by different team leads. Configure each approval action with a 4-hour timeout to ensure both approvals are collected within the time window.

Add a manual approval action in CodePipeline and configure the pipeline execution IAM role to require MFA from two separate IAM users. Attach a condition key in the approval IAM policy requiring aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent from at least two distinct principals.

explanation: Two sequential manual approval actions in CodePipeline require two separate approvals from different reviewers. Each action has its own timeout configuration, ensuring both must approve within the window. Option B uses a custom Lambda but CodePipeline manual approval actions natively support single approval only, so tracking dual approvals requires custom logic. Option C adds Step Functions complexity when sequential approvals are simpler. Option D's MFA conditions don't enforce dual-person approval on pipeline actions.

stem: A company needs to ensure that all EC2 instances launched in their AWS accounts have the AWS Systems Manager agent installed and are registered as managed instances. Some instances are launched from custom AMIs that don't include the SSM agent. Which approach ensures ALL instances become managed regardless of the AMI used?

options.text: Configure a default host management configuration in AWS Systems Manager that enables automatic SSM agent installation on all EC2 instances in the account. This uses the AmazonSSMManagedEC2InstanceDefaultPolicy to grant instances the necessary permissions without instance profiles.

Create a Lambda function triggered by EC2 RunInstances CloudTrail events via EventBridge. The Lambda function uses EC2 Instance Connect to SSH into new instances and install the SSM agent via remote command execution, then verifies registration in the SSM API.

Modify all Auto Scaling group launch templates to include a UserData script that downloads and installs the SSM agent from the S3 regional endpoint. Create an IAM instance profile with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy and attach it to the launch templates.

Create an AWS Config rule that checks if instances are registered as SSM managed instances. Configure auto-remediation with the AWS-ConfigureAWSPackage SSM document to install the SSM agent on non-compliant instances and register them with Systems Manager automatically.

explanation: Systems Manager Default Host Management Configuration automatically enables SSM management for all EC2 instances without requiring instance profiles or pre-installed agents. It handles agent installation and IAM permissions. Option A requires the SSM agent to already be installed for remediation to work, creating a chicken-and-egg problem. Option C uses Instance Connect which requires the Instance Connect agent and SSH access, adding complexity. Option D only covers Auto Scaling instances and doesn't handle manually launched instances.

stem: A company operates an Aurora PostgreSQL database that experiences read-heavy traffic spikes causing reader instances to become overwhelmed. Aurora Auto Scaling is configured but new read replicas take 5-10 minutes to become available. Which approach reduces the impact of sudden read traffic spikes?

options.text: Configure Aurora Auto Scaling with a lower target CPU utilization threshold of 40% to trigger scaling earlier. Add a predictive scaling policy based on historical traffic patterns and maintain a minimum of 3 reader instances during business hours via scheduled scaling actions.

Switch from Aurora PostgreSQL to Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 for the reader instances. Configure the minimum ACU to handle baseline read traffic and the maximum ACU to handle peak traffic, allowing automatic scaling in seconds instead of minutes for new instances.

Create additional Aurora cross-Region read replicas in a secondary Region. Configure the application's database connection pool to distribute read queries across both primary and secondary Region reader endpoints using DNS-based round-robin load balancing.

Add an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster between the application and Aurora for read caching. Implement a cache-aside pattern in the application code with a TTL matching the data freshness requirements, reducing the number of direct queries hitting Aurora readers.

explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 reader instances scale ACUs in seconds, eliminating the 5-10 minute provisioning delay of standard instances. This provides immediate capacity during sudden traffic spikes. Option A triggers scaling earlier but doesn't reduce the provisioning time. Option B adds caching which helps but requires application code changes and doesn't solve the database scaling speed issue. Option D adds cross-Region replicas which have replication lag and don't address the scaling speed for the primary Region.

stem: A company runs a multi-account AWS environment and needs to centralize security-related findings from Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Inspector, and Amazon Macie into a single dashboard for the security operations team. Which TWO configurations are needed?

options.text: Configure each service (GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie) to send findings to individual CloudWatch log groups in each account. Create cross-account CloudWatch log subscriptions to aggregate all findings into a central account's CloudWatch Logs for unified querying.

Enable the Security Hub integration with Amazon QuickSight in the central security account. Configure QuickSight to use the Security Hub findings data as a data source and build interactive dashboards with filters for finding severity, service, account, and time range.

Create custom EventBridge rules in each account that match security findings from all four services. Configure cross-account event bus targets to forward findings to a central security account's EventBridge bus and build a Lambda-based dashboard aggregation layer.

Designate a central security account as the AWS Security Hub delegated administrator through AWS Organizations. Enable Security Hub in all accounts with automatic enablement for new accounts and configure integration with GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie findings.

explanation: Security Hub as delegated administrator centralizes all security findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie across accounts (A). QuickSight integration provides the interactive dashboard with filtering capabilities for the security team (D). Option B routes findings through CloudWatch Logs losing the structured finding format that Security Hub provides. Option C builds custom aggregation when Security Hub already provides this natively.

stem: A company's ECS service running on Fargate experienced an outage because the tasks failed to pull a container image from Amazon ECR. Investigation revealed that a VPC endpoint for ECR was deleted during a network infrastructure update. Which proactive measure prevents this type of outage?

options.text: Create an AWS Config rule that monitors the existence of required VPC endpoints for ECR, S3, and CloudWatch Logs. Configure auto-remediation with an SSM Automation document that recreates the deleted VPC endpoints and updates the associated security group rules.

Configure CloudFormation stack policies on the network infrastructure stacks that deny Update:Delete actions on VPC endpoint resources. Apply the stack policy during stack creation and require a temporary policy override with change management approval for deletions.

Set up a CloudWatch alarm on the ECS service RunningTaskCount metric to detect when the count drops below the desired count. Configure the alarm to trigger an EventBridge rule that invokes a Lambda function to diagnose ECR connectivity and recreate endpoints.

Deploy the ECS service in public subnets with a NAT gateway as a fallback route for ECR image pulls. Configure the task definition with both the VPC endpoint and public internet ECR registry as image sources using a multi-stage Dockerfile with fallback layers.

explanation: CloudFormation stack policies prevent accidental deletion of critical resources like VPC endpoints by denying delete operations unless explicitly overridden. This proactively prevents the issue. Option A detects and remediates after deletion, but there's still a window where ECS tasks can't pull images. Option C reacts to the symptom (task count drop) rather than preventing the root cause. Option D uses public subnets and NAT gateways which contradicts the VPC endpoint architecture and adds cost.

stem: A company needs to implement a workflow where developers can assume elevated IAM roles for production troubleshooting, but only for 1-hour sessions, only after manager approval, and all actions must be logged with the developer's identity. Which solution implements this just-in-time elevated access?

options.text: Configure AWS Systems Manager Change Manager to define a change template for production access requests. When a manager approves the request, an SSM Automation runbook creates a time-limited IAM role policy with a 1-hour expiry condition and logs via CloudTrail.

Create an IAM role with an inline policy containing a time-based condition using aws:CurrentTime that restricts access to a 1-hour window. Have the developer request access through a Slack integration that calls a Lambda function to update the role's trust policy.

Create an IAM role with the required production permissions and a maximum session duration of 1 hour. Use AWS IAM Identity Center with a permission set that requires MFA and has a session duration of 1 hour, integrated with an approval workflow in ServiceNow via API.

Deploy a custom web application on API Gateway and Lambda that accepts access requests and sends approval emails to managers. Upon approval, the Lambda function calls the STS AssumeRole API to generate temporary credentials and delivers them to the developer securely.

explanation: SSM Change Manager provides a managed approval workflow where managers approve change requests, and SSM Automation creates time-limited access with full CloudTrail logging. Option A integrates external ServiceNow but IAM Identity Center doesn't natively include approval workflows. Option C builds a custom application that duplicates managed service functionality. Option D's time-based condition uses a fixed time window rather than a relative 1-hour session from the time of approval.

stem: A company uses AWS CodeBuild for their CI process. Build times are inconsistent, sometimes completing in 3 minutes and other times taking 15 minutes for the same codebase. Investigation reveals that the variance is caused by dependency downloads from public repositories. Which solution provides consistent build times?

options.text: Set up AWS CodeArtifact as a repository for upstream package registries including npm, PyPI, and Maven Central. Configure CodeBuild projects to use CodeArtifact as the package source, which caches upstream packages and serves them from within the AWS network.

Configure CodeBuild to use a VPC-attached build environment with a NAT gateway that has an Elastic IP. Set up a Squid proxy on an EC2 instance to cache downloaded dependencies and configure the build environment to use the proxy for all HTTP and HTTPS requests.

Create a custom Docker image containing all pre-installed dependencies and store it in Amazon ECR. Use this custom image as the CodeBuild environment image and rebuild the image weekly with updated dependencies using a scheduled CodePipeline pipeline.

Enable CodeBuild local caching with the source cache and custom cache modes enabled. Configure the S3 cache location to store dependency directories and set the cache expiry to 24 hours to ensure dependencies are refreshed daily from upstream repositories.

explanation: CodeArtifact acts as a managed package repository proxy that caches packages from upstream registries. Dependencies are served from within the AWS network, providing consistent download times. Option A adds proxy infrastructure complexity and requires VPC configuration. Option C's local caching may not persist across build environments if the underlying compute is different. Option D pre-installs dependencies but makes them stale between weekly rebuilds and requires image management.

stem: A company uses Terraform to manage infrastructure and wants to implement policy-as-code that prevents developers from creating overly permissive IAM policies (such as policies with '*' actions or '*' resources). The checks must run before terraform apply and block non-compliant changes. Which tool integrates with Terraform for this purpose?

options.text: Configure AWS IAM Access Analyzer policy validation to check IAM policies created by Terraform. Enable the Access Analyzer integration with the AWS provider and configure it to fail terraform plan when policy validation returns findings with ERROR severity level.

Use HashiCorp Sentinel with Terraform Cloud/Enterprise to write policy rules that inspect the terraform plan output for IAM policy documents containing '*' in actions or resources. Configure the Sentinel policies as hard-mandatory to block non-compliant applies.

Write custom Terraform validation blocks in the IAM policy resource definitions using the condition attribute. Define precondition checks that parse the policy JSON document and fail with an error message if any statement contains wildcard actions or resource ARNs.

Implement Open Policy Agent (OPA) with the Conftest tool to evaluate Terraform plan JSON output against Rego policies. Write Rego rules that parse IAM policy documents and deny plans containing wildcard permissions in action or resource fields.

explanation: HashiCorp Sentinel integrates natively with Terraform Cloud/Enterprise to evaluate plans against policy rules before apply. Hard-mandatory policies block non-compliant infrastructure changes. Option B uses OPA/Conftest which works but requires additional CI/CD integration rather than native Terraform workflow integration. Option C's IAM Access Analyzer works post-creation and doesn't integrate with terraform plan. Option D's validation blocks have limited expression support and can't parse complex JSON policy documents.

stem: A company operates a real-time data ingestion pipeline using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. The stream has 20 shards and receives 10,000 records per second. The company needs to ensure zero data loss even if the consumer application is down for up to 24 hours. Which configuration ensures data durability?

options.text: Configure the Kinesis stream with a retention period of 168 hours (7 days) to provide ample buffer beyond the 24-hour consumer downtime requirement. Enable server-side encryption using a KMS CMK and configure enhanced monitoring to track per-shard metrics.

Enable Kinesis Data Streams on-demand capacity mode to automatically scale shards based on throughput. Configure the stream with a retention period of 24 hours and use enhanced fan-out consumers to ensure dedicated throughput for each consumer application.

Deploy a Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream as an additional consumer that writes all records to an S3 bucket in real-time. Configure Firehose with a buffering interval of 60 seconds and enable S3 bucket versioning and server-side encryption for data durability.

Configure the producer application to write records to both Kinesis Data Streams and an SQS FIFO queue simultaneously. If the Kinesis consumer fails, configure a backup Lambda consumer to read from the SQS queue and reprocess the records into the pipeline.

explanation: Extending the Kinesis stream retention period to 168 hours ensures data is available in the stream for 7 days, well beyond the 24-hour recovery requirement. When the consumer recovers, it resumes from its last checkpoint. Option B adds S3 backup which provides durability but requires a different recovery mechanism than simply resuming the consumer. Option C sets retention to exactly 24 hours which leaves no safety margin. Option D adds dual-write complexity with SQS which is not necessary when stream retention handles the requirement.

stem: A company needs to implement real-time alerting on CloudTrail events that match specific patterns, such as root account logins, IAM policy changes, or security group modifications. Alerts must be delivered within 2 minutes of the event occurring. Which architecture provides the lowest latency alerting?

options.text: Configure CloudTrail to deliver events to an S3 bucket with event notifications enabled. Set up S3 event notifications to trigger a Lambda function that parses the CloudTrail log file and sends SNS notifications when matching patterns are found in the events.

Configure CloudTrail to deliver events to CloudWatch Logs with a log group in the same Region. Create CloudWatch Logs metric filters for each event pattern (root login, IAM changes, security group changes) and set up CloudWatch alarms with 1-minute evaluation periods.

Configure CloudTrail Lake to ingest all management events into the event data store. Create scheduled CloudTrail Lake queries that run every minute to search for root logins, IAM changes, and security group modifications, and publish results to an SNS topic.

Enable Amazon EventBridge integration with CloudTrail for management events. Create EventBridge rules with event patterns matching root account signin, IAM policy changes, and security group modifications, with SNS topics as targets for immediate notification delivery.

explanation: EventBridge receives CloudTrail management events in near-real-time and can match specific event patterns with rules, providing the lowest latency alerting. Option A uses CloudWatch Logs which has some delivery latency and requires metric filters. Option B has significant latency because CloudTrail delivers log files to S3 every 5-15 minutes. Option D uses scheduled queries which have at minimum 1-minute polling intervals and CloudTrail Lake ingestion latency.

stem: A company's Auto Scaling group frequently launches instances that fail health checks within 2 minutes of launch, causing a rapid cycle of launching and terminating instances. This results in high costs and inability to maintain the desired capacity. Which approach stabilizes the Auto Scaling group?

options.text: Switch the Auto Scaling group from ELB health checks to EC2 status checks to avoid premature termination. Configure a CloudWatch alarm on the Auto Scaling GroupInServiceInstances metric to alert when capacity drops below the desired count for investigation.

Increase the health check grace period on the Auto Scaling group to 600 seconds to allow more time for instance initialization. Configure the ALB target group health check with a longer interval of 30 seconds and increase the healthy threshold to 5 consecutive checks.

Enable Auto Scaling instance scale-in protection for all instances in the group to prevent termination. Configure a warm pool with a pool size equal to the desired capacity to maintain pre-initialized instances ready for immediate launch when failures occur.

Temporarily suspend the ReplaceUnhealthy Auto Scaling process to stop the launch-terminate cycle. Investigate the root cause by reviewing the instance system logs in the EC2 console and CloudWatch agent logs, then fix the underlying issue before resuming the process.

explanation: Suspending ReplaceUnhealthy stops the rapid launch-terminate cycle, allowing investigation of the root cause. Reviewing system logs and CloudWatch agent logs identifies why instances fail health checks. Option A increases wait time but doesn't address why instances are fundamentally failing. Option C changes to EC2 health checks which may mask application-level issues. Option D prevents scale-in but doesn't address the health check failures, and scale-in protection doesn't prevent replacement of unhealthy instances.

stem: A company needs to ensure that all Amazon EBS volumes are encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key. Existing unencrypted volumes must be identified and encrypted, and future unencrypted volume creation must be prevented. Which combination of actions achieves this?

options.text: Configure AWS CloudTrail to log CreateVolume API calls and create an EventBridge rule that triggers a Lambda function to encrypt newly created unencrypted volumes. Use Amazon Inspector to scan for unencrypted EBS volumes and generate findings for remediation.

Create an SCP that denies ec2:CreateVolume unless the aws:RequestTag/Encrypted condition is true. Deploy a Lambda function on a daily schedule that scans all EBS volumes using the DescribeVolumes API and creates encrypted copies of any unencrypted volumes found.

Implement a CloudFormation hook that validates EBS volume resources for encryption before stack operations. Deploy an AWS Config rule with auto-remediation that uses a Lambda function to snapshot, encrypt, and replace unencrypted volumes across all accounts.

Enable EBS encryption by default in each account's EC2 settings with the desired KMS CMK. Deploy an AWS Config rule encrypted-volumes to detect existing unencrypted volumes and use SSM Automation to create encrypted snapshots and replace unencrypted volumes.

explanation: EBS encryption by default ensures all new volumes are automatically encrypted with the specified CMK. AWS Config's encrypted-volumes rule identifies existing unencrypted volumes, and SSM Automation remediates them. Option B's SCP condition is incorrect as EBS encryption isn't controlled through request tags. Option C attempts post-creation encryption which doesn't work (you can't encrypt an existing unencrypted volume in-place). Option D uses CloudFormation hooks which only apply to CloudFormation-managed resources, missing volumes created through the console or API directly.

stem: A company needs to implement a GitOps workflow for their Kubernetes applications running on Amazon EKS. Application manifests are stored in a CodeCommit repository, and any change to the manifests should automatically sync to the EKS cluster within 5 minutes. Which approach implements this GitOps pattern?

options.text: Configure an EventBridge rule that matches CodeCommit repository state change events. Target a Lambda function that clones the repository, compares manifests against the cluster state using the Kubernetes API, and applies diffs using the kubectl binary in a Lambda layer.

Install Flux CD on the EKS cluster configured to watch the CodeCommit repository for manifest changes. Configure Flux with a sync interval of 1 minute and enable automated image updates with the Flux image automation controller for container image promotions.

Create a CodePipeline triggered by CodeCommit changes that runs a CodeBuild project to apply Kubernetes manifests. Configure CodeBuild with kubectl and the EKS cluster's kubeconfig to run kubectl apply on the changed manifest files from the repository.

Deploy ArgoCD on the EKS cluster and configure an Application resource pointing to the CodeCommit repository with a sync policy of automated pruning. Set the sync interval to 3 minutes and configure health checks for each Kubernetes resource in the application.

explanation: ArgoCD is a mature GitOps tool that continuously syncs Kubernetes manifests from Git repositories to EKS clusters with automated sync, pruning, and health checks. Option A uses Flux which also works for GitOps but has limited native CodeCommit support compared to ArgoCD. Option B uses a push-based CI/CD pipeline which is not true GitOps (GitOps requires pull-based reconciliation from the cluster). Option C implements custom sync logic in Lambda which is fragile and doesn't provide drift detection or continuous reconciliation.

stem: A company is using AWS CloudFormation and needs to create a stack that provisions resources in a specific order: first a VPC, then subnets, then an RDS instance in those subnets, and finally a Lambda function that needs the RDS endpoint. The RDS instance takes 15 minutes to provision. How should the template be structured to handle the dependencies and long provisioning time?

options.text: Create the VPC and subnets in one template deployed first. Use a separate template with a CloudFormation WaitCondition and WaitConditionHandle that pauses for 15 minutes before creating the Lambda function, allowing the RDS instance time to provision.

Split the resources into four nested stacks executed sequentially. Use CloudFormation stack outputs and Fn::GetAtt on AWS::CloudFormation::Stack resources to pass the VPC ID, subnet IDs, and RDS endpoint between nested stacks as parameters.

Define all resources in a single template without explicit DependsOn, relying solely on Fn::Ref and Fn::GetAtt intrinsic functions to establish implicit dependencies. CloudFormation automatically determines the correct creation order from these resource references.

Define all resources in the template with explicit DependsOn attributes creating the chain: VPC -> Subnets -> RDS -> Lambda. Use Fn::GetAtt to reference the RDS endpoint in the Lambda environment variables, which CloudFormation resolves after RDS creation completes.

explanation: CloudFormation automatically creates implicit dependencies when resources reference each other through Fn::Ref and Fn::GetAtt. No explicit DependsOn is needed when resource references exist. CloudFormation waits for each resource to complete before creating dependent resources. Option A adds unnecessary explicit DependsOn when implicit references handle the ordering. Option B adds nested stack complexity without benefit for linear dependencies. Option C uses WaitConditions with arbitrary timing instead of leveraging automatic resource dependency resolution.

stem: A company runs a critical API on Amazon API Gateway with a Lambda backend. During a Lambda service disruption in us-east-1, the API was completely unavailable for 45 minutes. The company requires an RTO of 5 minutes for this API. Which architecture provides the required resilience?

options.text: Deploy the Lambda function with provisioned concurrency in us-east-1 to ensure warm execution environments. Configure API Gateway with a caching layer and set the cache TTL to 300 seconds so that cached responses are served during Lambda service disruptions.

Deploy the API Gateway and Lambda function in both us-east-1 and us-west-2. Configure Route 53 with a failover routing policy and health checks on each Regional API Gateway endpoint. Route 53 automatically fails over to the healthy Region within 60 seconds of detection.

Deploy the Lambda function in us-east-1 and configure API Gateway with a Lambda@Edge function as a fallback integration. If the primary Lambda returns an error, configure API Gateway to retry the request against the Lambda@Edge function running in the nearest CloudFront edge location.

Deploy the API Gateway and Lambda function in us-east-1. Create an API Gateway Regional endpoint in us-west-2 as a standby and configure a CloudWatch alarm that triggers a Step Functions workflow to deploy the Lambda function to us-west-2 when disruption is detected.

explanation: Active-passive multi-Region deployment with Route 53 failover routing provides automatic Region failover within the health check interval (typically 60 seconds), meeting the 5-minute RTO. Option B uses caching which only works for GET requests and doesn't serve dynamic API responses during a full Lambda outage. Option C deploys Lambda on-demand during a disruption which exceeds the 5-minute RTO due to deployment time. Option D incorrectly uses Lambda@Edge which runs CloudFront functions, not as an API Gateway integration fallback.

stem: A company uses AWS Lambda functions that occasionally experience cold start latency exceeding 10 seconds for Java-based functions. The team needs to monitor cold start frequency and duration separately from warm invocation metrics. Which monitoring approach isolates cold start metrics?

options.text: Enable Lambda provisioned concurrency set to the expected baseline invocation rate. Monitor the ProvisionedConcurrencySpilloverInvocations CloudWatch metric to track how many invocations exceed provisioned capacity and experience cold starts during traffic spikes.

Configure AWS X-Ray tracing on the Lambda function and create a custom X-Ray group filtering for traces that include the Initialization subsegment. Use X-Ray analytics to compute the cold start percentage and average initialization duration across all traced invocations.

Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter on the Lambda function log group that matches the REPORT log line containing 'Init Duration'. Extract the init duration value as a custom metric and create alarms when the average cold start duration exceeds the 10-second threshold.

Enable Lambda Insights as a Lambda layer and configure the enhanced monitoring extension. Lambda Insights automatically reports Init Duration metrics separately from invocation duration, allowing CloudWatch dashboards to display cold start frequency and duration independently.

explanation: Lambda Insights extension automatically captures and reports Init Duration as a separate metric, providing direct visibility into cold start frequency and duration without custom configuration. Option B requires custom metric filter setup and only captures init duration from log text parsing. Option C uses X-Ray which provides trace-level detail but requires sampling and additional analysis. Option D uses provisioned concurrency which prevents cold starts rather than monitoring them, and spillover metrics don't measure actual cold start duration.

stem: A company's production DynamoDB table started returning ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors during a flash sale event. The table is configured with provisioned capacity and Auto Scaling with a target utilization of 70%. Which immediate action resolves the throttling while the team investigates capacity planning?

options.text: Increase the Auto Scaling maximum capacity units for both read and write capacity. Reduce the target utilization from 70% to 50% to trigger scaling earlier and configure the scaling cooldown period to 60 seconds for faster scale-up response during traffic surges.

Switch the DynamoDB table to on-demand capacity mode using the UpdateTable API. On-demand mode instantly adapts to traffic spikes by serving up to double the previous peak traffic, eliminating provisioned throughput exceptions without manual capacity adjustments.

Enable DynamoDB reserved capacity for the table at the expected peak read and write throughput. Configure CloudWatch alarms on ConsumedReadCapacityUnits and ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits to alert when consumption approaches 80% of the reserved capacity allocation.

Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table to absorb read traffic. Configure the DAX cluster with a cache TTL of 300 seconds and enable item-level caching for GetItem and BatchGetItem operations to reduce direct table read capacity consumption.

explanation: Switching to on-demand mode immediately handles the capacity issue by automatically scaling to accommodate any traffic level. It serves up to double the previous peak, ideal for flash sale spikes. Option B adjusts Auto Scaling parameters but scaling still takes minutes to react, too slow for flash traffic. Option C adds DAX for reads but the issue may involve write throttling too, and DAX deployment takes time. Option D's reserved capacity is a billing construct, not a capacity increase mechanism.

stem: A company stores sensitive customer PII in an Amazon S3 bucket. The security team needs to automatically discover and classify PII data, identify any PII that's been shared in public or cross-account S3 buckets, and generate compliance reports monthly. Which service combination meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure AWS Config rules with the s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited and s3-account-level-public-access-blocks rules. Use Amazon Textract to extract text from documents in the S3 bucket and apply custom regex patterns to identify PII fields in the extracted content.

Enable S3 Storage Lens with advanced metrics and recommendations to identify publicly accessible buckets. Configure S3 Inventory reports to list all objects and use Amazon Athena queries with regex patterns to scan inventory metadata for PII-related object key naming conventions.

Deploy Amazon Comprehend to analyze S3 objects for PII entities using the DetectPiiEntities API. Create a Lambda function to scan new objects triggered by S3 event notifications and store PII classification results in a DynamoDB table for monthly compliance reporting.

Enable Amazon Macie to scan the S3 buckets for PII using managed data identifiers. Configure Macie to generate sensitive data discovery results and use the Macie policy findings to identify publicly accessible or cross-account shared buckets containing PII.

explanation: Amazon Macie is purpose-built for PII discovery and classification in S3. It uses managed data identifiers for automated PII detection and policy findings identify public/cross-account exposure. Option B uses Comprehend which can detect PII in text but requires custom orchestration and doesn't analyze S3 access policies. Option C uses Config for access checks and Textract for OCR, but doesn't provide automated PII classification. Option D analyzes metadata and naming conventions but doesn't scan actual object content for PII.

stem: A company runs integration tests in their CodePipeline that require a fully deployed infrastructure environment. Creating the test environment takes 20 minutes and costs $50 per run. The team runs 30 pipeline executions daily. Which strategy reduces testing costs while maintaining test quality?

options.text: Create a persistent shared test environment that is reset between pipeline runs using CloudFormation stack updates. Configure CodePipeline to run integration tests against the shared environment and use a DynamoDB-based locking mechanism to serialize concurrent test executions.

Replace full integration tests with contract tests using Pact framework in a CodeBuild stage. Run lightweight consumer-driven contract tests that validate API interfaces between services without deploying full infrastructure, and run full integration tests only before production.

Configure CodePipeline with a manual approval gate before the integration test stage. Require developers to batch multiple code changes into a single pipeline execution and run integration tests only when explicitly approved, reducing the number of daily executions.

Use AWS CloudFormation with spot instances for the test environment infrastructure. Configure CodeBuild to create the environment using Spot Instance request templates and reduce the test suite to only critical path tests, cutting environment runtime by 50%.

explanation: Contract tests validate service interfaces without full infrastructure deployment, dramatically reducing cost and time while catching integration issues early. Full integration tests before production provide the final validation. Option A creates contention with a shared environment and serialized execution adds wait time. Option C reduces cost somewhat with Spot Instances but doesn't fundamentally change the $50-per-run economics. Option D delays feedback by batching changes and requiring manual approval, slowing development velocity.

stem: A company uses AWS CDK to define their infrastructure and wants to share a common set of constructs (VPC patterns, security configurations, monitoring setups) across 20 development teams. The shared constructs must be versioned and teams should be able to pin to specific versions. Which approach enables this shared construct library?

options.text: Build a shared CDK app that deploys common infrastructure (VPC, security, monitoring) to each account. Have teams import the deployed resources using Fn::ImportValue in their CDK stacks, creating cross-stack dependencies between the shared and team-specific infrastructure.

Create a CDK construct library as an npm package published to AWS CodeArtifact. Version the package using semantic versioning and configure each team's CDK project to reference the construct library as a dependency with a pinned version in their package.json file.

Create CloudFormation modules from the shared constructs and publish them to the CloudFormation registry as private modules. Have teams reference the modules in their CDK templates using CfnResource constructs with the module type and version constraints.

Store the shared CDK constructs in a central CodeCommit repository. Configure each team's CDK project to use git submodules referencing specific tags in the shared repository, and run cdk synth to verify construct compatibility during each team's CI/CD build.

explanation: Publishing CDK constructs as versioned npm packages to CodeArtifact provides a managed artifact repository with semantic versioning. Teams pin to specific versions in package.json, ensuring stability and controlled upgrades. Option B uses git submodules which are fragile, don't support proper dependency resolution, and require Git access configuration. Option C uses CloudFormation modules which lose CDK's programming benefits and L2/L3 construct abstractions. Option D shares deployed infrastructure, not reusable constructs, creating tight coupling between stacks.

stem: A company runs a stateless web application on an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB. During deployment, the team uses a rolling update strategy. Users report brief 502 errors during deployments because the ALB sends traffic to instances that are being terminated. Which configuration eliminates 502 errors during rolling deployments?

options.text: Add a lifecycle hook on the EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING event with a heartbeat timeout of 300 seconds. Configure the application to stop accepting new connections when it receives the termination signal and complete all in-flight requests before sending the CONTINUE signal.

Configure the Auto Scaling group with an instance refresh operation using a minimum healthy percentage of 100%. Set the instance warmup time to 300 seconds and configure the ALB health check with a 10-second interval and 5-second timeout for faster health detection.

Switch from a rolling update to a blue/green deployment strategy using CodeDeploy with an ALB. Configure CodeDeploy to create a replacement target group, shift traffic using ALB listener rules, and terminate original instances only after all connections are drained.

Configure the ALB target group deregistration delay to 120 seconds to allow in-flight requests to complete before instance termination. Set the Auto Scaling group's default cooldown to 300 seconds and enable connection draining on the target group for graceful shutdown.

explanation: Blue/green deployment with CodeDeploy creates a completely separate target group before shifting traffic, eliminating 502 errors caused by terminating instances receiving traffic. The old target group is fully drained before termination. Option A's deregistration delay helps but doesn't prevent the brief window where the ALB routes to terminating instances during rolling updates. Option C uses instance refresh which still performs rolling replacement and can cause brief errors. Option D adds lifecycle hooks but the ALB may still route traffic to the instance during the hook processing.

stem: A company needs to implement cost anomaly detection that alerts the finance team when any AWS service's daily spend increases by more than 20% compared to the 30-day average. The alert must include the specific service, account, and estimated impact. Which approach provides this cost monitoring?

options.text: Deploy a Lambda function on a daily schedule that queries AWS Cost Explorer API for service-level daily costs. Compare each service's cost against the 30-day rolling average and send formatted SNS notifications when any service exceeds the 20% threshold.

Configure AWS Cost Anomaly Detection with a monitor that tracks costs by AWS service. Set the alert threshold to 20% above the expected spend and configure SNS notifications to the finance team with anomaly details including service name, account ID, and root cause analysis.

Set up AWS Budgets with a daily cost budget for each AWS service and configure budget alerts at 120% of the 30-day average daily spend. Enable budget action notifications via SNS and configure the budget to include account-level breakdowns in the alert emails.

Create a CloudWatch alarm on the EstimatedCharges billing metric in us-east-1 with anomaly detection enabled. Configure the alarm to trigger when daily charges deviate by more than 20% from the expected band and send notifications via SNS with metric dimensions.

explanation: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses ML to detect spending anomalies by service and provides root cause analysis including the specific service, account, and estimated financial impact. Option B's CloudWatch billing metric provides aggregate estimated charges without service-level granularity. Option C requires pre-configured budgets per service and doesn't dynamically adjust baselines. Option D builds custom cost monitoring when a managed service provides this natively.

stem: During a Regional AWS service event, a company's application in us-east-1 became degraded. The team had no visibility into whether the issue was with their application or the AWS service. They need a way to quickly determine if AWS service issues are impacting their workloads during incidents. Which approach provides this visibility?

options.text: Deploy synthetic monitoring using CloudWatch Synthetics canaries that test critical application endpoints every minute. Compare canary failure patterns against the AWS Service Health Dashboard status page and create a custom dashboard showing both canary and service health side by side.

Subscribe to AWS Health Dashboard RSS feeds for all services used by the application. Configure a Lambda function to poll the feeds every minute and compare service health events against the application's error patterns stored in CloudWatch Logs for correlation analysis.

Enable AWS Health events integration with Amazon EventBridge in the application account. Create EventBridge rules that match health events for the services used (EC2, RDS, Lambda) and correlate them with application CloudWatch alarms using a centralized incident dashboard.

Configure Amazon CloudWatch Internet Monitor for the application's VPC endpoints. Monitor internet traffic paths for performance anomalies and use the Internet Monitor dashboard to distinguish between AWS infrastructure issues and application-level problems during incidents.

explanation: AWS Health events in EventBridge provide programmatic, account-specific notification of AWS service issues affecting your resources. Correlating health events with application alarms quickly identifies AWS service impact. Option A uses RSS feeds which are public and not account-specific, and polling introduces delay. Option C monitors internet paths, not AWS service health. Option D compares synthetic tests with the public dashboard which doesn't provide programmatic account-specific health data.

stem: A company needs to implement network-level isolation for their production EKS workloads. Different microservice teams should only be able to communicate with their own services and explicitly approved cross-team services. Which approach enforces this network segmentation within the EKS cluster?

options.text: Implement Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources with a default-deny ingress and egress policy in each namespace. Create specific NetworkPolicy rules that allow traffic only between pods with matching team labels and explicitly approved cross-team service selectors.
